body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students distinguish long-term causes from triggering events in explaining American expansion in 1898 and entry into the First World War (D2.His.15.9-12, D2.His.14.9-12).
- Students analyze wartime limits on free speech through the words of Eugene Debs, Woodrow Wilson and Justice Holmes, and how context shaped each perspective (D2.His.4.9-12, D2.Civ.12.9-12, RH.9-10.6).
- Students argue whether the United States should have joined the League of Nations, evaluating the role of treaties in keeping peace (D2.Civ.3.9-12, WHST.9-10.1).

MATERIALS
- Readings in the activities: Empire and War timeline, Anti-Imperialist League platform, Wilson's war message, Debs at Canton, Schenck v. United States, Fourteen Points Point XIV, The Senate and the League of Nations
- A large blank cause-and-effect chart with two columns: Long-term causes, Triggering events
- Optional: a public-domain map of the United States and its territories in 1900; public-domain World War I propaganda posters (Library of Congress)

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read A World Power. Brief lecture on 1898 with the timeline: why expand? Pair-read the Anti-Imperialist platform and the summary of the other side; class vote: should the United States have annexed the Philippines? Begin Why Did America Go to War?
Day 2: Finish Why Did America Go to War? and build the class cause chart. Discuss how the Zimmermann Telegram (trigger) differs from trade with Britain and France (long-term cause).
Day 3: Dissent in Wartime: read Wilson, Debs and Holmes. Socratic seminar on whether the government may punish speech that opposes a war. Note for teachers: the clear and present danger standard was later replaced; in Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) the Court held that the government may punish advocacy only when it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce it. Students begin the written analysis.
Day 4: Read The Senate and the League of Nations. Role-play the three Senate groups; then students draft Should America Have Joined the League?
Day 5: Unit assessment: Empire and War Unit Check (no AI help).

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: pre-sort the timeline events into causes and triggers for half the events; students sort the rest.
- Support: for the free speech sources, provide a paraphrase of each quotation and have students match it to the original before analyzing.
- Extension: read Justice Holmes's dissent in Abrams v. United States (1919), written months after Schenck, and explain how his view of free speech changed.
- Extension: research the Philippine-American War and compare its treatment in an older and a recent textbook (D2.His.6).
- Multilingual learners (ELL): use a visual timeline with icons for each event. Provide sentence frames: "A long-term cause was ___ because it built up over ___." "The trigger was ___ because it happened just before ___."

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
Our class is studying how the United States became a world power, from the Spanish-American War of 1898 through the First World War. We are asking hard questions: why do nations go to war, and should the government ever limit free speech during one? Ask your student about Eugene Debs, a presidential candidate who was sent to prison for a speech, and whether they think his conviction was fair. Thank you.
title: Teacher guide: Empire and the First World War
